html:
The capital of the Nabataeans, carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs in what is now southern Jordan. It is reached through the Siq, a narrow gorge more than a kilometre long. The chart's date, 312 BCE, is the first time the Nabataeans appear in history, when a Greek army attacked them.

The Nabataeans were Arab traders who controlled the northern end of the Incense trade route and grew rich taxing caravans of frankincense, myrrh and spices. In the desert they built dams, cisterns and clay pipes to catch and store the rare flash floods, so the city had water all year. Their tombs, such as the facade known as the Treasury, mix Greek and local styles.

In 106 CE the emperor Trajan annexed the kingdom to the Roman Empire. As trade moved to sea routes and other cities, Petra declined, and an earthquake in 363 did great damage. Europeans forgot it until the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812. It is now Jordan's most visited site.
